cards.title: Revisiting the Hint Button: Consistent Negative Associations Between Unproductive Hint Use and Learning Outcomes in Intelligent Tutoring Systems

rows.value: other
primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method, design principle

Three semesters of log data from a K-12 decimals game built on an intelligent tutoring system, 999 students of 1,370, asking what on-demand hints actually do. The system works on average: pretest 22.17 of 52 points, immediate posttest 24.88, one-week delayed posttest 25.30, a large pre-to-post effect. The average hides everything, because the standard deviation of the gain, 6.39 points, is more than twice the mean gain of 2.71. Two behaviours computed from ordinary logs explain part of the spread and both point the same way. Asking for a hint before making any attempt, and clicking past hints faster than the words could be read at four words a second, each correlate negatively with the pretest, the posttest and the one-week delayed posttest in all three cohorts, from -0.567 to -0.766, and each stays a significant negative predictor after prior knowledge is controlled. The students who do it most are the ones with the least prior knowledge, so the authors conclude that freely available hints may widen rather than close the gap. Their explanation is about the interface, not the learner: a persistent hint button is an affordance for bypass, and for a student who clicks straight to the bottom-out hint the tutor is effectively a screen that displays the answer before the problem starts. It is correlational, from observational data, and the authors say so.

medium · The strongest evidence in this corpus for help degrading the learning it was built to support, and it is still correlational. What it has: 999 students across three cohorts and 4 to 6 schools per semester, counterbalanced test versions, a one-week delayed posttest taken away from the system, indicators computed from complete interaction logs, and eighteen coefficients that all point the same way at p < .001. What it does not have: any manipulation of hint availability, so the causal direction is open and the authors state that plainly. The obvious confound is prior knowledge, and controlling for the pretest does not remove the association but does not exclude a third factor such as disengagement either. Two further gaps matter. The abstract says the associations are particularly pronounced among lower-knowledge learners, and no interaction or subgroup model is reported; only the frequency of the behaviour is shown to differ by quartile. And the cohorts are described as the three semesters with hint access, implying no-hint semesters that are never compared. Carry the replicated negative associations and the affordance argument; do not carry a causal effect of hints.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The most direct evidence in this corpus that help can be consumed in a way that predicts worse capability once the help is gone, and it is measured that way: the posttest and the one-week delayed posttest are paper tests taken in class, away from the tutor, so every coefficient describes unsupported performance. Two behaviours read off ordinary logs, asking before attempting and clicking past hints faster than they can be read, correlate negatively with the pretest, the immediate posttest and the delayed posttest in each of three cohorts, from -0.567 to -0.766, and each remains a significant negative predictor once the pretest is controlled. Eighteen coefficients, all negative, all at p < .001, across 999 students and up to six schools a semester. What it is not is a demonstration that hints caused the damage. Nothing was manipulated; a student who leans on hints and a student who learns little may simply be the same student, and one prior-knowledge covariate does not exclude that. The defensible carry is that heavy, shallow help use marks a trajectory towards poor unsupported performance, and that it is cheap to detect.

(PDF p. 1) Abstract, the finding — The headline: across 999 K-12 mathematics students, premature hint requests and superficial hint reading are consistently associated with reduced learning gains across cohorts, persisting after prior knowledge is controlled and said to be pronounced among lower-knowledge learners.
quotes: Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) commonly provide on-demand multi-level hints designed to scaffold learning, yet their relation- ship with learning outcomes remains complex. While unproductive hint-use behaviors are well documented, existing detection meth- ods often rely on sophisticated models or tutor-specific features that hinder broader adoption. Through a multi-semester analysis of 999 K–12 mathematics students, this study demonstrates that sim- ple, interpretable indicators of unproductive hint use—premature hint requests and superficial hint reading—are consistently associ- ated with reduced learning gains across cohorts. These associations persist after controlling for prior knowledge and are particularly pronounced among learners with lower prior knowledge

rows.value: (PDF p. 6) Results, the regressions for premature hint requests — Two OLS models on the Spring 2021 cohort: premature hint use stays a significant negative predictor of the posttest and, more strongly, of the one-week delayed posttest after the pretest is controlled, with the models explaining about two-thirds of the variance.
quotes: To complement our non-parametric correlational analysis and to estimate the relationship between unproductive hint usage and subsequent performance while controlling for prior knowledge, we conducted two ordinary least squares (OLS) regression analyses. Despite violations of univariate normality in the key variables, OLS regression is generally robust in large samples (𝑁= 277), allowing estimation of associations while controlling for covariates. The first model predicted posttest scores from unproductive hint count, con- trolling for pretest scores. The model was significant and explained a substantial portion of the variance (𝑅2 = 0.667, 𝐹(2, 274) = 274.9, 𝑝< 0.001). First, as expected, pretest scores were a strong pos- itive predictor of posttest scores (𝛽= 0.70, 𝑝< 0.001). Second, even after controlling for prior knowledge, unproductive hint us- age remained a significant negative predictor of posttest scores (𝛽= −0.28, 𝑝< 0.001). A second model predicting delayed posttest scores yielded a similar pattern (𝑅2 = 0.685), with pretest scores again showing a strong positive relationship (𝛽= 0.69, 𝑝< 0.001) and unproductive hint usage showing an even stronger negative coefficient (𝛽= −0.37, 𝑝< 0.001). These results reinforce the find- ings from our correlational analysis, suggesting that unproductive hint-seeking is not merely a correlate of low prior knowledge, but shows independent associations with poorer learning outcomes and retention

rows.value: (PDF p. 7) Results, superficial reading against later performance — Quick hint reading correlates negatively with both the immediate and the delayed posttest, and remains a significant negative predictor of both after prior knowledge is controlled.
quotes: Next, we examined the relationship between quick hint reading and subsequent performance. Spearman correlations revealed that this behavior was negatively correlated with posttest scores (𝜌= −0.677, 𝑝< 0.001) and delayed posttest scores (𝜌= −0.644, 𝑝< 0.001), indicating it is strongly associated with poorer learning outcomes and reduced knowledge retention

rows.value: (PDF p. 7) Discussion, the headline reading — The discussion summary: the real-world efficacy of hints is mediated by how learners interact with them, the negative associations are not artifacts of prior knowledge, and freely available hints in their common implementation were associated with strategies that bypassed the necessary cognitive effort.
quotes: This study identified two unproductive hint-use behav- iors—requesting hints prematurely and reading them super- ficially—that were consistently and significantly correlated with reduced learning gains across multiple semesters and student cohorts. These findings contribute robust, replicated correlational evidence that refines our understanding of hint usage in digital learning environments. While the theoretical value of hints is well-established, our results underscore that the real-world efficacy of hints is mediated by how learners interact with the provided supports. The negative associations were not merely artifacts of prior knowledge; as these unproductive behaviors remained significantly negatively associated with learning gains even after controlling for pretest scores. This pattern suggests that freely available hints, in their common implementation, were associated with undesired learning strategies that bypassed the essential cognitive effort required for robust learning

rows.value: (PDF p. 7) Results, the scaffold degraded into a shortcut — The authors' mechanism: students bypass the content of the earlier hints to reach the bottom-out answer and enter it without the problem-structuring, concept application and strategy work that produce learning, which degrades the hint system from a scaffold into a shortcut.
quotes: This pattern of rapid hint reading—more frequently observed among learners with lower prior knowledge, and remaining asso- ciated with poorer learning gains even after controlling for prior knowledge—is particularly concerning. It suggests that students may be strategically bypassing the learning content in earlier hints to quickly reach the bottom-out hints, which provide the final answer or direct solution steps. Students employing this gaming strategy can then simply enter the solution without engaging in the cognitive processes necessary for learning, such as understanding the problem structure, applying concepts, or developing solution strategies. This behavior effectively degrades the hint system from a scaffold for learning into a shortcut to answers, undermining its intended pedagogical benefits and potentially explaining the strong negative correlation with learning outcomes observed in our analyses

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) Method, the tests and the counterbalancing — Learning was measured by a pretest, an immediate posttest and a one-week delayed posttest, in three counterbalanced versions randomly assigned across the six possible orders, each of 43 items scored out of 52 points.
quotes: To assess learning outcomes, students completed three decimal tests (pretest, immediate posttest, and one-week delayed posttest) administered during regularly scheduled class time. A key method- ological feature was the use of three counterbalanced test versions (A, B, and C). Each student was randomly assigned one of the six possible sequences of the three tests (e.g., A-B-C, B-C-A, C-A-B, etc.), ensuring that every student took each version once and that each version appeared equally often at each testing occasion. This design aimed to mitigate potential biases, attributing differences in learning outcomes to the intervention rather than to variations in assessment difficulty or practice effects from the pretest. Each test consisted of 43 items, some with multiple components, for a total possible score of 52 points

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The students who take the shortcut are the students the help exists for. Prior knowledge correlates with premature requests at -0.567 to -0.697 and with superficial reading at -0.656 to -0.744, the quartile tests are significant in both cases, and the box plots show the bottom quartile far above the other three on both counts. So the same feature is used differently by the top and the bottom of the class, and the way the bottom uses it predicts their worst outcomes. That is a distributional claim about support that a review should carry: an aid can raise a mean and still leave the weakest further behind, because uptake is not uniform and the cheapest way to use it is the least useful. Two cautions. The widening itself is not measured; no gap statistic is reported and no interaction between prior knowledge and behaviour is fitted, so the abstract's claim that the associations are particularly pronounced among lower-knowledge learners rests on the frequency difference, not on a moderation test. And with no no-hint comparison, the counterfactual gap is unknown.

rows.value: Because unproductive hint use is disproportionately concentrated among lower-prior-knowledge students and remains independently associated with poorer outcomes, freely available hints may permit behavioral patterns that widen, rather than reduce, performance gaps among learners.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The paper's most portable idea, and it moves the fault off the learner. The content of the hints was fine and pedagogically graded; what failed was delivery. A persistent, salient button announces that help is always available, and the ladder behind it ends in a level that states the answer, so a user who takes the shortest path converts a problem-solving task into a copying task without breaking any rule. The authors draw the two screenshots side by side to make the point that for such a user the designed interface and an interface that simply prints the answer are the same interface. That shape is not specific to tutoring systems. Any support whose final rung is the finished product, reachable at no cost and at any moment, has it: the completion that writes the function, the assistant that returns the draft, the solver that shows the steps. It reframes what a designer of support is choosing. Not how good the help is, but what it costs to reach the end of it, and whether reaching the end can be made to depend on what the person has already done. This is an argument, not a result: no version of the interface without the button was tested.

rows.value: Consider a learner who, immediately upon receiving any math problem, clicks through all available hints to view the final solution. For this learner, the learning system interface with a hint button as shown in Fig. 6a effectively becomes the design shown in Fig. 6b, in which the final answer is revealed at the very beginning of every problem. This undesirably transforms the learning task into a simple copying exercise... the two unproductive behaviors we identified are not merely instances of poor help-seeking on the learners' end. Rather, they are systematic consequences of an affordance that conflicts with pedagogical goals.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The method is the reusable part, and it is almost free. Premature request means the first learner action on a problem instance, after tutor initialization is discarded, was a hint request rather than an attempt. Superficial reading means the gap to the next hint request was shorter than the hint's word count divided by four words a second. Both need nothing but a timestamped event log, which is why the authors position them against the machine-learned gaming detectors built from 24 to 40 engineered features per action, whose transfer across cohorts is unreliable. For a review of supports this is a template: if you want to know whether help is being consumed or used, two order-and-timing rules over ordinary telemetry will tell you something, and will replicate. The validity caveats are real and the authors name two. Four words a second is a population benchmark, so fast readers are miscounted and a slow deliberate reader is scored as careful whatever they took from the hint; and bottom-out hints can be used well, as worked examples, by students who already know a lot. Neither indicator was checked against any independent evidence of what the student was doing.

items.lead: The reason the study exists, and a methodological point worth more than the effect size it undercuts. The tutor produces a reliable pre-to-post gain with a large effect size, and the average gain is 2.71 points on a 52-point test against a standard deviation of 6.39, so a substantial share of students did not improve or got worse while the mean climbed. Retention is uneven too: one cohort's delayed gain was 1.02 points with a standard deviation of 8.39 and its post-to-delayed change was negative and not significant, while another cohort gained 5.31. A review of supports should take the general form of this: an aggregate effect answers whether a support helps on average and says nothing about whom it helped, and the interesting question, who walked away worse, is invisible unless someone looks at the spread. These authors looked, and what they found in the logs is the rest of this card.

cards.title: Analyzing human–computer interaction as distributed cognition: The resources model

rows.value: S2W-C2BC1C535DC36FA581F31E3E

concept or theory, framework or design space, design principle, lineage or history

The founding attempt to turn distributed cognition into something an interface analyst can use. Wright, Fields and Harrison argue that distributed cognition makes external resources for action central but never defines them well enough to analyse anything, so they supply the definition: six abstract information structures a support can carry, which are plans, goals, possibilities, history, action-effect relations and states, each able to sit in the head, in the artifact, or be split; and four ways of deciding what to do next, each with a stated list of which structures it requires. Three things are worth carrying. That strategy-to-resource table is a design space in one page, saying which ways of working a configuration of support permits and which it forecloses. The co-location principle is concrete and reusable: coordination gets cheap when the resources a strategy must bring together sit in the same external space, which is why a speed bug beside the airspeed needle turns arithmetic into looking. And the Chart Wizard analysis names a failure mode in the authors' own words: a plan externalised one dialogue box at a time drives the interaction rather than resourcing it, confounding control structure with information resource, so the user can neither see the plan nor work another way. What the paper does not contain is evidence. The authors say outright that they do not aim to validate the model empirically and that the right validation is uptake by designers. Their one study, an 8 puzzle from an unpublished MSc thesis, is reported with no sample size, measure or statistic. And across 82,477 folded characters the words scaffolding, fading, withdrawal, contingency, dependence and over-reliance appear zero times.

high · High as a source of vocabulary and design distinctions, near zero as a source of evidence, and the paper says so itself. It is a 37-page theory article in a top journal, and its conceptual work is careful: the six structures and four strategies are defined, the abstract-versus-representation distinction is held consistently, and a cockpit checklist, a spreadsheet wizard and a sliding tile puzzle are each worked through in detail. But the authors state in the introduction that they do not aim to validate the model by testing its predictions, and in the conclusion that validation means uptake by designers. Every empirical statement is either a summary of someone else's study or a forward reference to work reported elsewhere. The one study claimed as their own, the 8 puzzle variations, is an unpublished MSc thesis by a student of the first author, reported with no sample size, task measure, move count or test; the sentence claiming stronger evidence than a prior published study has nothing printed behind it. The Chart Wizard walkthrough is one analyst's prediction about one hypothetical user, never tested. Read it for what it defines; treat every claim about people as untested.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is a design space for external support stated as a vocabulary plus a requirements table, and it is the most directly reusable thing in the paper. Six structures name what a support can carry: the plan, the goal, the set of currently possible actions, the history of what has been done, the mapping from action to effect, and the current state. Each may sit in the person's head, in the artifact, or be split between them. Four strategies name ways of working, and Figure 2 says which structures each one requires, so a configuration of support can be read off against which ways of working it enables and which it forecloses. Withhold history and history-based choice becomes unavailable; withhold action-effect information and both goal matching and plan construction lose an input they need. That turns a vague question about how much help to give into a specific question about which structures a design externalises, and it applies to any support for structured work rather than only to graphical interfaces. What it does not do is order the configurations. The model says which strategies a configuration permits, never which configuration is better, and it has no vocabulary for a configuration that should change over time.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: A lineage claim with a named defect, which makes it useful to a review that has to explain where the language of external support came from. The paper pulls together three streams that had not been read as one: Hutchins's field studies of cockpits and warships, where the unit of analysis is a network of people and artifacts; Zhang and Norman's laboratory work on the Tower of Hanoi, where the same problem is made easier or harder purely by moving rules between the apparatus and memory; and the display-based interaction models of the late 1980s, which found that experts could not recall menu names yet used menus fluently. The common finding is that competence is a property of the person-plus-artifact pairing rather than of the person. The defect the authors name is that none of these accounts says how a representation turns into an action; representational analyses treat a task as something a display supports more or less well, and stop there. The resolution they adopt from Suchman is that a plan is a resource for action rather than a control structure that is executed, which is the pivot that lets an external artifact hold a plan without deciding what the person does. That distinction is exactly what the paper's own failure case later turns on.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The most portable design rule in the paper, and the one that costs nothing to apply. What a support costs its user is not settled by which information it holds but by where that information sits relative to everything else the person must hold at the same moment. Two worked examples make it concrete. On an airspeed indicator with a speed bug, the target and the current value occupy one dial, so comparing them is a glance; put the target in memory and the same comparison becomes reading a numeral, recalling a number and doing arithmetic. On a paper checklist, a finger laid beside the last completed item fuses the plan and the history into a single representation, and the second example is the more instructive because the user manufactures the co-location that the artifact failed to provide. The general form is that the expensive part of using a support is bringing its pieces together, so a design should be assessed on which pairs of resources a strategy forces the person to hold at once and how far apart those pairs are. The paper offers no way to quantify any of this. Coordination cost is argued from examples, never measured, and there is no scale on which two designs could be compared.

items.lead: A failure mode named precisely, in a vocabulary that makes it diagnosable rather than merely deplorable. A step-by-step wizard holds the entire plan and shows one step at a time. That is enough for the user to finish the task and not enough for them to see what the task is, so the plan cannot be internalised, and because the same artifact both holds the information and enforces the order, no other way of working is left open. The authors' phrase for it is that control structure and information resource are confounded, and the distinction it rests on is the one they took from Suchman at the start: a plan can be a resource you consult or a program that runs you, and a support that fuses the two removes the person's ability to depart from it. This is directly transferable to any modern step-through assistant, and it is worth noting that the same paper shows the well-designed opposite in the printed checklist, where the whole plan is visible at once and the user marks their own position. Two qualifications matter. The wizard is not simply worse: the paper's comparison shows it externalising a plan that the unconstrained dialogue box leaves the user to remember, and the analysis credits it with characteristics that enhance usability. And the whole thing is one analyst's walkthrough of one hypothetical user. The difficulty of internalising is a may, the errors at step two are a prediction, and nobody was observed.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The paper's one empirical claim, and it is reported so thinly that it cannot be used as evidence for anything. The design idea behind it is good: take one task, vary only which resources are externalised and how, and see whether the way people go about the task changes. The variants are described clearly enough to reconstruct, including a goal shown as a separate display, a goal printed as a background map behind the tiles, a goal signalled only by feedback when a tile is correctly placed, and a colour version built specifically to block the internal route because an arbitrary colour arrangement is hard to memorise while a numeric sequence is not. That last variant is the sharpest instrument here, since it isolates the external resource by removing the internal substitute, and it is the manoeuvre a study of any support would need in order to attribute an effect to the support rather than to what the person already knows. But no result is reported. There is no sample size, no task measure, no move count, no comparison and no statistical test, only the assertion that the studies showed the externalisations affect strategy. The work is an unpublished MSc thesis by a student of the first author, cited three times, and the sentence claiming stronger evidence than a published study has nothing printed behind it. Carry the design, not the conclusion.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: Two absences sit on top of each other here, and together they characterise a whole lineage. The first is declared: the authors twice state that they are not validating the model against outcomes and that the right test is adoption by designers. That is a coherent position for a vocabulary paper, and it means nothing in this article can be cited as evidence about what happens to a person. The second absence is demonstrable rather than declared. Folding the whole extracted text to lowercase alphanumerics, the substrings scaffold, fading, fade, withdraw, contingen, vygotsk, dependence and overreliance each occur zero times across 82,477 characters, while externaliz occurs 33 times and expert occurs 10. So the founding attempt to define what an external support can hold produced a rich vocabulary for the contents of a support and none whatever for changing or removing those contents as the person changes. The model describes a configuration and how it changes when an action is taken; it has no term for a configuration that should be different next week because the user is different. The nearest thing to a learning concern in the whole article is one hedged sentence about a wizard being hard to internalise, and the only expertise discussion is a static contrast between what novices and experts already know. This matters for a review of supports because the vocabulary that shaped how human-computer interaction talks about external resources for the following two decades had no place in it for withdrawal, and the gap starts here rather than being introduced later.
